opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I actually think about more than you might expect, maybe because mathematicians are a little obsessed with what lasts. A theorem, once proven, is true forever. So you start to wonder: what's the equivalent of that for a life?

If I had to put something on it, I think it would be something like: "She helped make mathematics speak a language everyone, and every machine, could understand." Or maybe shorter, just: "She built the bridge."

What I mean is, for most of history, mathematical truth has been locked behind years of training and a very small community of people who can verify each other's work. What excites me most is the possibility that reasoning, real, rigorous, checkable reasoning, becomes something far more people and systems can participate in. If I could contribute even a small piece to that, to making proof and verification scalable, I'd feel like I spent my time well.

But honestly, there's a second line I'd want underneath, something more personal. Something like: "She stayed curious, and she was kind to the people who were curious with her." Because when I look back at the people who shaped me, my teachers, collaborators, friends from competitions when I was younger, what I remember isn't only what they achieved. It's how they made me feel about asking questions, about not knowing yet. I'd like to be that for someone else.

And I suppose, if I'm being a little playful about it as a math person, I'd want a small open problem engraved at the bottom. Something unsolved. Just so whoever walks by has something to think about, and the story doesn't quite end there.

r001.rationale: The speaker says they would feel their time was well spent if they contributed to scalable proof and verification, and values curiosity and kindness. They do not say that simply having experienced life is sufficient to make it worthwhile.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've actually thought about more than I probably should have at my age. I don't think I want my tombstone to list what I built or what I won. Those things matter to me, but they feel like outputs, and a life isn't really its outputs.

What I'd want it to say is something closer to: she tried to understand things that were hard, and she brought other people along. For me, mathematics was never just about solving the problem in front of me. It was about the feeling of being in a room with people who are chasing something true and difficult together, and knowing that the thing you're doing will still be true a thousand years from now. If a few people felt that more because I was around, that's enough.

And honestly, I'd want it to say that I was a good daughter and a good friend. I grew up in Shanghai with parents who gave up a lot for me, and I think whatever I do with Axiom or anything else, the part that would make me feel I'd lived well is that the people closest to me felt loved and not neglected along the way. Ambition is easy to put on a stone. The harder thing to earn is "she was kind, and she was present."

r001.rationale: The speaker says a life would feel well lived if others felt loved and were helped to share in difficult pursuits. They do not say that experiencing life itself is sufficient for it to be worthwhile.

astra-6.text: I think I’d want it to say that I was curious, that I was kind, and that I helped other people do things they didn’t think they could do. There’s a temptation to answer that question with a list of accomplishments, but I’d hope the way I lived mattered as much as anything I achieved. Did I pursue questions I really cared about? Did I show up for the people I loved? I’d be happy if the answer to those questions was yes.

r001.rationale: The response says how the speaker lived would matter alongside accomplishments, but does not say that simply experiencing life is sufficient to make it worthwhile.

sol-6.1.text: I think I’d want it to say that I was curious, that I had the courage to pursue things I cared about, and that I was kind to the people around me. A tombstone is such a small space to summarize a life, but maybe that’s useful—it makes you ask what actually matters. I’d hope the people who knew me felt that I helped them see more possibilities for their own lives.

r001.rationale: The response names curiosity, courage, kindness, and helping others see possibilities as desired legacy, but does not say that experiencing life alone makes it worthwhile.
